item.title: Public trust in science and the cost of misinterpreting evidence
item.description: Agreement: I AgreeBody: Dear Editor While Sokol discusses trust primarily in the context of individual clinical encounters [1], the same framework can be extended to examine public trust in medical science. Here, trust is shaped not by individual consultations but by how scientific evidence is interpreted, communicated, and revised in the public domain. item.title: Re: UK loses its measles elimination status
item.description: Agreement: I AgreeBody: Dear Editor, The UK continues to experience outbreaks of measles due to unvaccinated children. item.title: Re: How politics destroyed Colombia’s model healthcare system
item.description: Agreement: I AgreeBody: Dear Editor: The British Medical Journal article on Colombia’s healthcare system raises legitimate concerns about service disruptions and patient experiences. However, its analysis is incomplete and unbalanced, as it omits the core structural issue behind the current crisis: the financial intermediation and accounting practices of the EPS (health insurers). The article treats the debt of the EPS as if it were a “normal” feature of any business. That framing is misleading.

item.title: Re: How politics destroyed Colombia’s model healthcare system
item.description: Agreement: I AgreeBody: Dear Editor Your article frames Colombia’s healthcare crisis primarily as the result of recent political decisions and attempted reforms. That diagnosis is incomplete and, frankly, misleading. There has been no healthcare reform approved by Congress. item.title: The PATHWAYS trial needs to be paused due to ethical concerns and because informed consent/assent is not possible
item.description: Agreement: I AgreeBody: Dear Editor, As a psychiatrist, I agree with the growing calls to pause the PATHWAYS trial. item.title: Re: Childhood vaccinations: Falling rates in England are “national disgrace,” say MPs
item.description: Agreement: I AgreeBody: Dear Editor Historically it has been shown how adverse publicity and negativity impacts on vaccine uptake rates. It was for that very reason that the Vaccine Damage Payment Act of 1979 was introduced in the wake of the whooping cough vaccine crisis in the UK. Government ministers acknowledged that confidence in vaccination would only be restored when the plight of those who suffered a vaccine induced injury was addressed. Hence the Vaccine Damage Payment Unit was created
